newsitem.title: JORDAN: Israel cancels gas joint venture with Jordan.
newsitem.headline: Israel cancels gas joint venture with Jordan.

text.p: A Israeli-Jordanian joint venture to set up a $300 million gas plant hit a snag Sunday after Jordanian officials said Sunday that Israel formally pulled out of the deal which was spearheaded by Enron Corp.
The gas plant at Jordan's Red Sea port of Aqaba would have supplied the two countries with gas from the Gulf.

"The project is non-existent...the new Israeli government is apparently not interested in the project any longer," said Energy Minister Hashem Dabbas in an interview, adding that Israel had probably opted for other sources of gas.
Israeli Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon's office responded that the Jewish state had not cancelled the deal.

"Sharon emphasises Israel did not cancel any project and it is ready to discuss with any element the supplying of gas to Israel, including with...Qatar and Enron which proposed supplying liquefied gas," it said in a statement.

"A letter clarifying this position was sent...to the Qatari foreign minister....The Infrastructure Ministry continues to check various possibilities to bring natural gas and electricity on a cost benefit basis also from other sources."
The gas plant was designed to bring liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the Gulf state of Qatar to Israel and Jordan in the first quarter of 2001.

The deal was agreed at a Middle East economic summit two years ago amid a wave of optimism about Arab-Isreali economic cooperation. But Israel's enthusiasm for the project appeared to wane in the following months.

Investors say the Israeli government's reluctance was based on economics. They say Israel believes getting LNG from Qatar by vessels was more expensive than other sources including direct pumping of gas from Egypt.
Israel's previous Labour government strongly lobbied for the project, despite opposition of some Israeli industrial groups, to help draw Jordan closer economically and consolidate peace.
The project grew out of an initial understanding between Enron and Israel reached in October 1995 in Amman for the supply of at least two million metric tons of Qatari gas to Israel.

Originally Israel was to get an estimated 75 percent of gas and Jordan the remaining 25 percent. The plant was to have taken two years to construct with the first Qatari gas deliveries to Jordan and Israel by the first quarter of 2001.
Jordanian investors said Enron had been notified by Israel late last year that it no longer was interested in the project.

The joint venture in which Jordanian and Israeli investors were to hold an equal 25 percent equity share with Enron holding a 50 percent was formally registered in Jordan and Israel but never capitalised, investors said.
The project was the largest undertaking planned so far between the Israeli and the Jordanian private investors since a peace treaty in 1994 that ended a 46-year state of war.

Investors say a collapse of the project would be a serious setback to efforts to create large private sector joint ventures between the two states that would create a common interest in preserving peace.
